newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Tamil parties question Sri Lankan president's plan.
newsitem.headline: Tamil parties question Sri Lankan president's plan.

text.p: Tamil political parties backing Sri Lankan President Chandrika Kumaratunga have started to challenge her policies over the country's ethnic issues, party leaders said on Monday.

Some Tamil party leaders said they will not support a coordinating committee that Kumaratunga set up last week to address problems in the predominantly Sinhalese island's north and east, home to many minority Tamils.
"We have decided to boycott the committee," said Douglas Devananda, leader of the Eelam People's Democratic Party (EPDP), the largest Tamil political party in parliament.
"I don't think the committee could efficiently handle problems of Tamil people. The government has not met our demand to form an interim administration in the north and east," he told Reuters.

EPDP is one of three Tamil parties represented in parliament that say Tamils, particularly the more than 250,000 who recently returned to their homes in the military-controlled northern Jaffna peninsula, face hardship and human rights abuses.

Government forces recaptured Jaffna, 320 km (220 miles) north of Colombo, in April after Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE) rebels had ruled the region for almost a decade with their own administration, courts and police.

EPDP, and the Peoples Liberation Organisation for Tamil Eelam (PLOTE), which also opposes the committee, backs the government's fight against the LTTE. The rebels want a separate homeland in the north and east.

The Tamil parties criticise the rebels' attacks on civilians and economic targets, such as the bombing of the Central Bank this year that killed about 100 people. They also support the government's peace plan offering greater autonomy to the Tamils.
Tamil party leaders said, however, the president's committee would not be effective.

"People may think the committee is an interim administration in another name," Devananda said. "But the committee to be led by the centre will not be able to address the problems of the Tamil people."

Kumaratunga appointed Shipping, Ports, Rehabilitaton and Reconstruction Minister M.H.M. Ashraff to head the committee -- one of the reasons Devananda and PLOTE leader Dharmalingam Sithadthan cite for boycotting the panel.

"We wanted an interim council to fill the vacuum in political decision-making to reflect the wishes of the Tamil people," Sithadthan said. "The government did not consult with us for the committee and we reject it out of hand."
Devananda said: "Again it comes under the central government, while we are speaking of the devolution of power."
The Tamil leaders have backed the government's bid to revise the constitution, offering to devolve wide-ranging powers to Tamils, who make up about 17 percent of 18 million Sri Lankans.
The peace package, under consideration by a parliamentary select committee, aims to end the 13-year war that the government says has killed more than 50,000 people.
Progress on the package has been stalled by the main opposition United National Party (UNP), which opposes a proposal for federalism to replace the current unitary state formula.

The UNP, with 85 seats in Sri Lanka's 225-seat parliament, is key to the peace package's success because a two-thirds majority is required. The three Tamil parties, which together have 17 seats, have so far voted for the government.
